title: Responsible AI: fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security
learningObjective: Describe considerations for fairness, reliability and safety, and privacy and security in an AI solution, and the practices that address them.
foundation: AI systems make predictions and generate content that affects real people. Microsoft defines six principles for responsible AI; this lesson covers the first three.
Fairness: the system should treat everyone fairly. A loan model shouldn't approve one group less often than a similar group without good reason.
Reliability and safety: the system should work as intended, also in unusual situations, and fail safely instead of causing harm.
Privacy and security: protect the data used to train and run the system, respect people's privacy, and defend against attacks.
engineer: Fairness risks: biased training data (under-represented groups), sensitive attributes or proxies (postcode standing in for ethnicity), and different quality of service (speech recognition that works worse for some accents). Harms include allocation (jobs, loans) and quality-of-service gaps.

Fairness practices: review data for representation, compare selection and error rates across groups (for example with the Responsible AI dashboard's fairness assessment), remove or justify proxy features, and keep testing after changes.

Reliability and safety risks: unexpected inputs, edge cases, model drift, hallucinations in generative AI, and harmful outputs. Practices: evaluate before release (Foundry evaluations for quality and safety), red-team with adversarial prompts, set content filters and guardrails, keep humans in the loop for high-impact decisions, monitor in production, and define a safe fallback.

Privacy and security risks: personal data in training data, prompts or logs; data leakage; prompt injection and jailbreaks. Practices: collect only what you need and get consent, detect and redact PII (Azure Language PII detection), use Microsoft Entra ID and private networking, keep keys in Key Vault, and use Prompt Shields to detect direct and indirect prompt attacks.

In Microsoft Foundry, prompts and completions sent to models are not used to train the foundation models, and data stays in your Azure tenant and chosen geography (see each service's data privacy documentation).

example.title: A loan pre-screening assistant
body: A bank's model approves applicants from one postcode area far less often. The fairness assessment shows postcode acting as a proxy; the team removes it and re-tests error rates per group.
Before launch they red-team the chat assistant, set content filters and a 'transfer to a person' fallback, and redact account numbers from logs.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription with access to Microsoft Foundry (ai.azure.com)
permissions: Azure AI User to run evaluations; Azure AI Project Manager to change guardrails
limits: Model availability differs by region and deployment type
Deployments have tokens-per-minute (TPM) rate limits and quota per subscription and region
portal: Foundry portal > Guardrails + controls: content filters and Prompt Shields.
Foundry portal > Evaluation: run quality and safety evaluations on a model or agent.
Open a model card to read intended uses and limitations.

lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.symptom: A speech app works poorly for some accents.
troubleshooting.cause: Unrepresentative training or test data (quality-of-service gap).
troubleshooting.fix: Test with diverse speakers; use custom speech with representative data.
Redact PII before logging and limit retention.

comparisons.difference: Fairness is equal treatment in outcomes; inclusiveness is designing so everyone can use the system.
Safety prevents the system causing harm; security protects it from attackers.

misconceptions.myth: Removing the sensitive attribute guarantees fairness.
misconceptions.reality: Proxies can carry the same bias.

misconceptions.myth: A highly accurate model is safe.
misconceptions.reality: Rare failures and harmful outputs still need guardrails.

misconceptions.myth: Data sent to Foundry models trains them.
misconceptions.reality: Your prompts aren't used to train foundation models.

architectureDecisions: Minimise and protect personal data end to end.
